claim: Recessive mutations in WDR62 are responsible for the second most frequent form of MCPH.
source: Recessive mutations in WDR62, located on chromosome 19, are responsible for the second most frequent form of MCPH (Bilgüvar et al., 2010, Nicholas et al., 2010, Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Bilgüvar et al., 2010, Nicholas et al., 2010, Yu et al., 2010).

claim: WDR62 is a spindle pole-associated protein involved in mitotic progression and NPC maintenance.
source: WDR62 is a spindle pole-associated protein involved in mitotic progression and NPC maintenance (Bogoyevitch et al., 2012; Novorol et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; Jayaraman et al., 2016; Sgourdou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: WDR62 plays an important role in the assembly and disassembly of the primary cilium.
source: In addition, it is thought to play an important role in the assembly and disassembly of the primary cilium (Zhang et al., 2019; Shohayeb et al., 2020), an antenna-like structure able to sense and convey extracellular cues guiding NPC proliferation versus differentiation (Wilsch-Bräuninger and Huttner, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Zhang et al., 2019; Shohayeb et al., 2020).

claim: The subcellular localization of WDR62 varies during the cell cycle and is regulated by its N- and/or C-terminal domains and microtubule association.
source: The subcellular localization of WDR62 varies during the cell cycle and is regulated by its N- and/or C-terminal domains and microtubule association (Bogoyevitch et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2015; Ramdas Nair et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: In interphase, WDR62 localizes to the centrosome via stepwise hierarchical interactions with other MCPH-associated proteins, including CDK5RAP2 and CEP63.
source: Notably, in interphase, WDR62 is reported to localize to the centrosome via stepwise hierarchical interactions with other MCPH-associated proteins, including CDK5RAP2 and CEP63 (Kodani et al., 2015; O'Neill et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kodani et al., 2015; O'Neill et al., 2022).

claim: A homozygous 4 bp deletion in exon 23 of WDR62 leads to a frameshift and a premature stop codon, resulting in a C-terminally truncated protein (D955AfsX112).
source: Whole exome sequencing identified a homozygous 4 bp deletion in exon 23 of WDR62, leading to a frameshift and a premature stop codon, which results in a C-terminally truncated protein (D955AfsX112) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole exome sequencing data and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutant WDR62 (D955AfsX112) fails to localize to the mitotic spindle poles in Mut iPSCs.
source: We found that mutant WDR62 remained diffuse and failed to localize to the mitotic spindle poles in Mut iPSCs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Het and CTRL iPSCs, WDR62 co-localized with PCNT and TUBA1A at the spindle poles.
source: In contrast, in Het and CTRL iPSCs, WDR62 co-localized with PCNT (pericentrin) and TUBA1A (tubulin alpha 1a) at the spindle poles (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), similarly to our previous findings in skin fibroblasts (Sgourdou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, and by citation to a previous study (Sgourdou et al., 2017).

claim: Spindle pole localization of WDR62 was restored in Iso 1 iPSCs.
source: As expected, spindle pole localization was restored in Iso 1 iPSCs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WDR62 was detected as a polarized perinuclear signal during interphase, localized around the centrosome in G1-S Mut iPSCs.
source: We also detected WDR62 as a polarized perinuclear signal during interphase, which appeared to be localized around the centrosome (marked by PCTN) in G1-S Mut iPSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: WDR62 localizes to the Golgi apparatus during interphase in iPS-NES cells.
source: WDR62 localized to the Golgi apparatus (GOLGA1/Golgin 97-positive) in interphase Iso 2 and Mut iPS-NES cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Full-length and mutant WDR62 localized to the Golgi apparatus at comparable amounts in iPS-NES cells.
source: Analysis of fluorescence signal intensity suggested that full-length and mutant WDR62 localized to the Golgi apparatus at comparable amounts, potentially excluding a non-physiological accumulation of the mutant protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During mitosis, the WDR62 signal was centered on discrete regions corresponding to the spindle poles in Iso 2 iPS-NES cells.
source: During mitosis, the WDR62 signal was centered, as expected, on discrete regions corresponding to the spindle poles in Iso 2 iPS-NES cells, while the Golgi apparatus was scattered around the chromatin, appearing as clusters formed during mitosis that are eventually partitioned between daughter cells (Ayala et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B and by citation to a published study (Ayala et al., 2020).

claim: In Mut iPS-NES cells, the WDR62 signal was diffuse during mitosis, with a large fraction (60%) overlapping with GOLGA1.
source: In contrast, in Mut iPS-NES cells the WDR62 signal was diffuse (Figure 2B), with a large fraction (60%) overlapping with GOLGA1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and co-localization analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: No WDR62 signal was detected in WDR62-silenced iPS-NES cells, indicating antibody specificity.
source: No signal was detected in WDR62-silenced cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating antibody specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: WDR62 co-localized with GOLGA1 in 58.2%±8.9 of Golgi ministacks after nocodazole-induced fragmentation.
source: Remarkably, we observed that WDR62 co-localized with GOLGA1 in 58.2%±8.9 of ministacks (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), thus confirming its tight association with the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi fragmentation experiments and co-localization analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: FLAG epitope-tagged full-length WDR62 co-localized with GALT1-mWasabi at the Golgi apparatus in interphase iPS-NES cells.
source: We observed co-localization of FLAG and mWasabi signals, similar to the endogenous WDR62 and Golgi apparatus (GOLGA2+) signals (Figure 2B), thus corroborating WDR62 presence in the organelle in interphase cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-transfection experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Two additional WDR62 pathogenic mutations (W224S and V1402GfsX12) prevent WDR62 localization to the mitotic spindle poles but allow localization to the Golgi apparatus.
source: We extended these observations by testing with the same approach two additional WDR62 pathogenic mutations, N-terminal missense W224S and C-terminal frameshift V1402GfsX12, encountered in patients with MCPH2 (Bilgüvar et al., 2010). In both cases, the FLAG signal was absent from the mitotic spindle poles, but detected at the Golgi apparatus (mWasabi and GOLGA2+), similar to the pattern observed for the D955AfsX112 mutation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-transfection experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, D and by citation to a published study (Bilgüvar et al., 2010).

claim: WDR62 localized to the spindle poles of mitotic RG-like cells in Iso 2 and Het, but not Mut, COs.
source: WDR62 localized to the spindle poles of mitotic RG-like cells in Iso 2 and Het, but not Mut, COs (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C.

claim: The Golgi apparatus is polarized toward the ZO-1+ apical domain of RG-like cells within neural rosettes in human COs.
source: We observed a radial distribution of the Golgi apparatus, polarized toward the ZO-1+ apical domain of the RG-like cells within the neural rosettes (Figure 2—figure supplement 7A), where WDR62 was also confined (Figure 2—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7A and 7B.

claim: WDR62 and GOLGA1 highly co-localized to the apical domain of RG-like cells during interphase in Iso 2, Het, and Mut COs.
source: We also found that WDR62 and GOLGA1 highly co-localized to the apical domain of the RG-like cells during interphase in Iso 2, Het, and Mut COs (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and co-localization analysis shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The WDR62 signal was enriched in the apical side of RG-like cells with comparable relative fluorescence values in Iso 2, Het, and Mut COs.
source: Of note, the WDR62 signal was enriched in the apical side of RG-like cells with comparable relative fluorescence values in Iso 2, Het, and Mut COs (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2G.

claim: FLAG epitope-tagged full-length and mutant WDR62 co-localized with GALT1-mWasabi in RG processes in the developing mouse neocortex.
source: Finally, we delivered FLAG epitope-tagged full-length or mutant (D955AfsX112, V1402GfsX12, W224S) WDR62 and GALT1-mWasabi to the developing neocortical wall of the mouse at embryonic day (E) 13.5 by in utero electroporation. We observed overlapping FLAG and mWasabi signals in RG processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by in utero electroporation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Following nocodazole treatment, WDR62 appeared diffuse around the nucleus in mitotic Iso 2 iPS-NES cells and was absent from the spindle poles and the centrosomal/pericentrosomal area.
source: Following nocodazole treatment and fixation, WDR62 appeared diffuse around the nucleus in mitotic Iso 2 iPS-NES cells and was absent from the spindle poles and the centrosomal/pericentrosomal area, stained with CETN2 (Degl'Innocenti et al., 2022) or PCTN (Figure 3A); the same pattern was observed in Mut iPS-NES cells (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by nocodazole treatment experiments shown in Figure 3A and by citation to a published study (Degl'Innocenti et al., 2022).

claim: The percentage of WDR62 and GOLGA1 co-localization was similar in nocodazole-treated Iso 2 and Mut iPS-NES cells.
source: Moreover, the percentage of WDR62 and GOLGA1 co-localization was similar in nocodazole-treated Iso 2 and Mut iPS-NES cells (Figures 2C and 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figures 2C and 3B.

claim: Microtubules are fundamental for the Golgi apparatus-to-spindle pole translocation of WDR62 during mitosis.
source: Together, these observations strongly suggest that microtubules are fundamental for the Golgi apparatus-to-spindle pole translocation of WDR62 during mitosis and that the C-terminal part of the protein may have an important role in the interaction of WDR62 with microtubules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nocodazole treatment experiments and the observation that the mutation prevents spindle pole localization.

claim: CDK5RAP2 was correctly localized to the centrosome during mitosis and interphase in Mut iPS-NES cells.
source: We found that both during mitosis and interphase, CDK5RAP2 was correctly localized, as we reported previously for skin fibroblasts (Sgourdou et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and by citation to a previous study (Sgourdou et al., 2017).

claim: CDK5RAP2 was localized to the centrosome during G1 and before centriole duplication in Iso 2 iPS-NES cells, whereas WDR62 remained associated with the Golgi apparatus.
source: We found that, already during G1 and before centriole duplication, CDK5RAP2 was localized to the centrosome, whereas WDR62 remained associated with the Golgi apparatus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) both in untreated and in nocodazole-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After centriole duplication at early S-phase, only CDK5RAP2 was detected at the centrosomes both in untreated and in nocodazole-treated cells.
source: After centriole duplication at early S-phase (Holland et al., 2010), only CDK5RAP2 was detected at the centrosomes both in untreated and in nocodazole-treated cells, even before the centrioles started to migrate to participate in spindle pole formation (O'Neill et al., 2022; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and by citations to published studies (Holland et al., 2010; O'Neill et al., 2022).

claim: In nocodazole-treated cells during prometaphase, CDK5RAP2 remained at the centrosome, whereas WDR62 appeared dispersed.
source: In nocodazole-treated cells, however, the two proteins showed divergent behavior: CDK5RAP2 remained at the centrosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), whereas WDR62 appeared dispersed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: The D955AfsX112 mutation did not prevent WDR62 interaction with CDK5RAP2 in a co-immunoprecipitation assay.
source: We found that the mutation did not prevent WDR62 interaction with CDK5RAP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) or with AURKA or TPX2 (Lim et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2016) in a similar overexpression/co-IP assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and by citations to published studies (Lim et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2016).

claim: The D955AfsX112 mutation did not prevent WDR62 interaction with AURKA or TPX2 in a co-immunoprecipitation assay.
source: We found that the mutation did not prevent WDR62 interaction with CDK5RAP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) or with AURKA or TPX2 (Lim et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2016) in a similar overexpression/co-IP assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G and by citations to published studies (Lim et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2016).

claim: The mutation does not impinge WDR62 binding to several of its physical interactors, but prevents shuttling to the spindle poles.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the mutation does not impinge WDR62 binding to several of its physical interactors, but prevents shuttling to the spindle poles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments and the observation that the mutation prevents spindle pole localization.

claim: At 9 pcw in the cortical plate, the WDR62 signal was polarized and perinuclear, overlapping with GOLGA2.
source: At 9 pcw in the cortical plate (CP), where committed neuroblasts are populating the incipient cortical layers, the WDR62 signal was polarized and perinuclear, overlapping with GOLGA2, thus retracing the pattern observed in non-mitotic iPS-NES cells (Figure 4B' and B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data of human fetal telencephalic tissue shown in Figure 4B' and B''.

claim: In the cortical ventricular zone at 9 pcw, WDR62 was detected at the TUBA1A-positive spindle poles in mitotic cells.
source: In the cortical ventricular zone (VZ), where RG cells reside and most mitotic events occur, WDR62 was detected at the TUBA1A-positive spindle poles in mitotic cells (Figure 4B' and B'''); in contrast, the WDR62 signal appeared elongated and scattered in interphase cells, reminiscent of the distribution of the Golgi apparatus along radial processes in COs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, A').
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data of human fetal telencephalic tissue shown in Figure 4B' and B'''.

claim: At 11 pcw, the WDR62 and GOLGA2 signals were polarized and perinuclear in the CP and in the mantle zone of the developing striatum.
source: Similarly, in human fetal incipient dorsal and ventral telencephalic areas at 11 pcw (Figure 4D), the WDR62 and GOLGA2 signals were polarized and perinuclear in the CP (Figure 4D and D' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, B') and in the mantle zone of the developing striatum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B''), but scattered and localized in the CTNNB1+ (beta catenin) apical processes in RG cells at the germinative zones (Onorati et al., 2014; Castiglioni et al., 2019; Figure 4D' and D'' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B', B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data of human fetal telencephalic tissue shown in Figure 4D, D', and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, B', B'' and by citations to published studies (Onorati et al., 2014; Castiglioni et al., 2019).

claim: WDR62 and GOLGA2 signal co-localization was persistent at 9 and 11 pcw, showing a perinuclear and polarized pattern at the CP and a radial/apical pattern at the VZ.
source: Thus, we found persistent WDR62 and GOLGA2 signal co-localization at 9 and 11 pcw, showing a perinuclear and polarized pattern at the CP, consistent with the distribution of the Golgi apparatus in post-mitotic neurons (Taverna and Huttner, 2019), and a radial/apical pattern at the VZ (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data of human fetal telencephalic tissue shown in Figure 4F and by citation to a published study (Taverna and Huttner, 2019).

claim: WDR62 and GOLGA1 displayed a high incidence of co-localization at the VZ/SVZ, IZ/SP, and CP.
source: Independently from area-specific patterns, WDR62 and GOLGA1 displayed a high incidence of co-localization at the VZ/subventricular zone (SVZ), intermediate zone (IZ)/subplate (SP), and CP (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization analysis of human fetal telencephalic tissue shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There were significantly fewer MKI67+ cells in Mut iPS-NES cell cultures compared to Iso 1 and Iso 2.
source: We found significantly fewer MKI67+ (also known as Ki-67) cells in Mut iPS-NES cell cultures (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The reduction in MKI67+ cells suggests a tendency for premature cell cycle exit in Mut iPS-NES cells.
source: Since MKI67 detects cells at all phases of the cell cycle except G0, this result suggests a tendency for premature cell cycle exit in Mut iPS-NES cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduction in MKI67+ cells and the known function of MKI67.

claim: There were no significant differences in the global mitotic index (PH3+/total cells) between Iso 1, Iso 2, and Mut iPS-NES cells in unsynchronized cultures.
source: On the other hand, we did not find significant differences in the global mitotic index (PH3+/total cells) between Iso 1, Iso 2, and Mut iPS-NES cells in unsynchronized cultures (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The distribution of mitotic figures was not significantly different in unsynchronized Iso 1, Iso 2, and Mut iPS-NES cell cultures.
source: Before nocodazole treatment (T0), we did not find statistically significant differences in mitotic figure distribution (i.e. cells at each mitotic phase, evaluated through PH3 staining), between Iso 1, Iso 2, and Mut iPS-NES cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After nocodazole treatment, the percentage of Mut iPS-NES cells in prometaphase was reduced at T1 but increased at T2.
source: In contrast, the percentage of Mut iPS-NES cells in prometaphase was reduced at T1 but increased at T2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Approximately 80% of Iso 1 and Iso 2 iPS-NES cells arrested in prometaphase at T1 had re-entered the cell cycle at T2.
source: We found that approximately 80% of Iso 1 and Iso 2 iPS-NES cells arrested in prometaphase at T1 had re-entered the cell cycle at T2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After an insult affecting mitotic progression, Mut iPS-NES cells are delayed compared to Iso counterparts.
source: Altogether, our data confirm that after an insult affecting mitotic progression, Mut iPS-NES cells are delayed compared to Iso counterparts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the synchronization experiments.

claim: There were no differences in inter-centrosomal distance (ICD) between Iso 1, Iso 2, and Mut iPS-NES cells.
source: We found no differences in ICD, but a smaller spindle angle α in Mut iPS-NES cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mut iPS-NES cells had a smaller spindle angle α compared to Iso 1 and Iso 2 iPS-NES cells.
source: We found no differences in ICD, but a smaller spindle angle α in Mut iPS-NES cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Primary cilia appeared significantly shortened in Mut iPS-NES cells, compared to Iso 2 counterparts.
source: We found that primary cilia appeared significantly shortened in Mut iPS-NES cells, compared to Iso 2 counterparts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: RG-like progenitors in Mut COs displayed asymmetric cell divisions more frequently, suggestive of premature differentiation.
source: We found that RG-like progenitors in Mut COs displayed asymmetric cell divisions more frequently, suggestive of premature differentiation (Kosodo et al., 2004; Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I and by citation to a published study (Kosodo et al., 2004).

claim: The incidence of symmetric and asymmetric divisions was comparable in Het and Iso 2 COs.
source: On the other hand, the incidence of symmetric and asymmetric divisions was comparable in Het and Iso 2 COs (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: WDR62 is important for maintaining proliferative divisions in RG-like progenitors.
source: These observations suggest that WDR62 is important for maintaining proliferative divisions in RG-like progenitors and that the mutation results in a shift toward neurogenic divisions in COs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased incidence of asymmetric divisions in Mut COs.

claim: The mutation results in a shift toward neurogenic divisions in COs.
source: These observations suggest that WDR62 is important for maintaining proliferative divisions in RG-like progenitors and that the mutation results in a shift toward neurogenic divisions in COs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased incidence of asymmetric divisions in Mut COs.

claim: There was an increase in mitotic index in Mut versus Iso 2 neuroectodermal cells at DIV16.
source: Quantification of MKI67+ and PH3+ mitotic cells, as well as EdU-incorporating S-phase cells, revealed an increase in mitotic index in Mut versus Iso 2 neuroectodermal cells at DIV16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TBR1+ and BCL11B+ neurons were significantly enriched in Mut compared with Iso 2 iPSC-DIV40 cultures.
source: We observed a significant enrichment in early-born neurons expressing TBR1 and BCL11B (also known as CTIP2), markers of layers 6 and 5, respectively, in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV40 cultures (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There were no differences in the percentage of MAP2+ cells between Iso 2 and Mut iPSC-DIV40 cultures.
source: No differences emerged in the percentage of MAP2+ cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TUBB3 density was increased in Mut compared with Iso 2 iPSC-DIV40 cultures, suggesting premature differentiation.
source: However, the total TUBB3+ surface area normalized to the total cell number (DAPI+), defined as TUBB3 density, was increased in Mut compared with Iso 2 iPSC-DIV40 cultures (Figure 6C), suggesting premature differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There were significantly fewer TBR1+ and late-born SATB2+ neurons in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures.
source: Conversely, we observed significantly fewer TBR1+ and late-born SATB2+ (layer 2/3), but now comparable BCL11B+, neurons in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: BCL11B+ neurons were comparable between Iso 2 and Mut iPSC-DIV80 cultures.
source: Conversely, we observed significantly fewer TBR1+ and late-born SATB2+ (layer 2/3), but now comparable BCL11B+, neurons in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TUBB3 density was no longer different between Mut and Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures.
source: Moreover, TUBB3 density was no longer different between Mut and Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: At DIV40, Mut neuroderivatives had, on average, longer TUBB3+ neurites compared to Iso 2 counterparts.
source: At DIV40 we found, on average, longer TUBB3+ neurites in Mut neuroderivatives with respect to their Iso 2 counterparts, while at DIV80 the difference appeared to be resolved, suggesting a possible early neuronal maturation, but not final neuronal morphometric differences between genotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At DIV80, the difference in average neurite length between Mut and Iso 2 neuroderivatives appeared to be resolved.
source: At DIV40 we found, on average, longer TUBB3+ neurites in Mut neuroderivatives with respect to their Iso 2 counterparts, while at DIV80 the difference appeared to be resolved, suggesting a possible early neuronal maturation, but not final neuronal morphometric differences between genotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a significant increase in average neurite length from DIV40 to DIV80 only in Iso 2 cultures.
source: By cross-comparing DIV40 and DIV80 time points, we found a significant increase in average neurite length only in Iso 2 cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There were fewer mature neurons expressing RBFOX3 in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures.
source: Moreover, we found fewer mature neurons expressing the pan-neuronal marker RBFOX3 (also known as NeuN) in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), however, both contained terminally differentiated neurons expressing the presynaptic marker synaptophysin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both Iso 2 and Mut iPSC-DIV80 cultures contained terminally differentiated neurons expressing synaptophysin.
source: Moreover, we found fewer mature neurons expressing the pan-neuronal marker RBFOX3 (also known as NeuN) in Mut compared to Iso 2 iPSC-DIV80 cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), however, both contained terminally differentiated neurons expressing the presynaptic marker synaptophysin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was a reduction in GABAergic interneurons in Mut iPSC-DIV80 derivatives.
source: Lastly, we observed a reduction in GABAergic interneurons, but a normal proportion of GFAP-expressing astrocytes in Mut iPSC-DIV80 derivatives (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was a normal proportion of GFAP-expressing astrocytes in Mut iPSC-DIV80 derivatives.
source: Lastly, we observed a reduction in GABAergic interneurons, but a normal proportion of GFAP-expressing astrocytes in Mut iPSC-DIV80 derivatives (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: WDR62 regulates NPC fate and differentially impacts the neurogenic trajectories of neuronal subclasses.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that WDR62 regulates NPC fate and differentially impacts the neurogenic trajectories of neuronal subclasses, potentially recapitulating the abnormalities in neocortical cytoarchitecture observed in WDR62 mouse model (Sgourdou et al., 2017) and MCPH patients.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differentiation experiments and supported by citation to a previous study (Sgourdou et al., 2017).

claim: WDR62 associates with the Golgi apparatus during interphase in iPS-NES cells.
source: Our analyses employing these models demonstrated that WDR62: (i) associates with the Golgi apparatus in interphase neural progenitors and mouse and human fetal telencephalon
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: WDR62 translocates to the spindle poles during the interphase-to-mitosis transition in a microtubule-dependent manner.
source: Our analyses employing these models demonstrated that WDR62: (i) associates with the Golgi apparatus in interphase neural progenitors and mouse and human fetal telencephalon; (ii) translocates to the spindle poles during the interphase-to-mitosis transition in a microtubule-dependent manner
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: WDR62 regulates mitotic progression and asymmetric versus symmetric divisions in neural progenitors.
source: Our analyses employing these models demonstrated that WDR62: (i) associates with the Golgi apparatus in interphase neural progenitors and mouse and human fetal telencephalon; (ii) translocates to the spindle poles during the interphase-to-mitosis transition in a microtubule-dependent manner; (iii) regulates mitotic progression and asymmetric versus symmetric divisions in neural progenitors
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: WDR62 regulates NPC fate.
source: Our analyses employing these models demonstrated that WDR62: (i) associates with the Golgi apparatus in interphase neural progenitors and mouse and human fetal telencephalon; (ii) translocates to the spindle poles during the interphase-to-mitosis transition in a microtubule-dependent manner; (iii) regulates mitotic progression and asymmetric versus symmetric divisions in neural progenitors; and (iv) regulates NPC fate.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal half (aa 955–1523) of WDR62 likely regulates WDR62-microtubule interactions required for translocation.
source: As pharmacological disruption of microtubules in isogenic corrected iPS-NES cells prevents WDR62 from translocating to the spindle poles, we are prompted to propose that the C-terminal half (aa 955–1523) of the protein likely regulates WDR62-microtubule interactions required for translocation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nocodazole treatment experiments and the location of the mutation.

claim: Both the N- and C-terminal halves of WDR62 play important roles, respectively, binding to and regulating interactions with microtubules.
source: Together, these results suggest that both the N- and C-terminal halves of WDR62 play important roles, respectively, binding to and regulating interactions with microtubules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experiments with multiple mutations and the nocodazole treatment experiments.

claim: The Golgi apparatus regulates mitotic spindle formation by promoting the activation of TPX2.
source: It is worth noting that the Golgi apparatus regulates mitotic spindle formation by promoting the activation of TPX2 (Wei et al., 2015), a spindle assembly factor that has been reported to interact with the middle region of WDR62 (Chen et al., 2014); this interaction, however, does not appear to be disrupted by the D955AfsX112 mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Wei et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2014).

claim: TPX2 is a spindle assembly factor that has been reported to interact with the middle region of WDR62.
source: It is worth noting that the Golgi apparatus regulates mitotic spindle formation by promoting the activation of TPX2 (Wei et al., 2015), a spindle assembly factor that has been reported to interact with the middle region of WDR62 (Chen et al., 2014); this interaction, however, does not appear to be disrupted by the D955AfsX112 mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Chen et al., 2014).

claim: The interaction between WDR62 and TPX2 does not appear to be disrupted by the D955AfsX112 mutation.
source: It is worth noting that the Golgi apparatus regulates mitotic spindle formation by promoting the activation of TPX2 (Wei et al., 2015), a spindle assembly factor that has been reported to interact with the middle region of WDR62 (Chen et al., 2014); this interaction, however, does not appear to be disrupted by the D955AfsX112 mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Impairment of cell cycle and propensity for asymmetric cell divisions in NPCs underscore altered neurogenic processes, ultimately resulting in MCPH.
source: Considered together, these observations suggest a dynamic and microtubule-dependent shuttling of WDR62 from the Golgi apparatus to the spindle poles. Several pathogenic mutations prevent this process and, therefore, WDR62 localization at the spindle poles during mitosis, thus impacting, in turn, NPC fate and regulation of neurogenic trajectories. Our findings further reinforce the notion that cell cycle impairment and propensity for asymmetric cell divisions in NPCs underscore altered neurogenic processes, ultimately resulting in MCPH (Jayaraman et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Jayaraman et al., 2018) and by the findings of the manuscript.

claim: In vitro models of human neurodevelopment derived from patient cells harboring pathogenic mutations are particularly valuable for mechanistic understanding of brain development and pathology.
source: Our results demonstrate that in vitro models of human neurodevelopment derived from patient cells harboring pathogenic mutations are particularly valuable for mechanistic understanding of brain development and pathology, pointing to promising avenues of investigation with broad applications to medicine.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the successful use of patient-derived iPSCs in the study.

claim: Iso 2 and Mut iPS-NES cells expressed comparable levels of WDR62 mRNA.
source: Iso 2 and Mut iPS-NES cells expressed comparable levels of WDR62 mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Full-length (165 KDa) and mutant (118 KDa) WDR62 protein were detected by western blot in CTRL iPS-NES cells overexpressing the respective constructs.
source: we were able to detect by western blot the full-length and mutant protein overexpressed in CTRL iPS-NES cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Spindle pole localization of WDR62 was previously shown to require AURKA-mediated phosphorylation of the WDR62 N-terminal half (aa 1–790).
source: Spindle pole localization was previously shown to require AURKA-mediated phosphorylation of the WDR62 N-terminal half (aa 1–790) (Lim et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Lim et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2021).

claim: Multiple mutations throughout WDR62, including at the C-terminus, have been found to impair localization of endogenous or overexpressed mutant WDR62 to the spindle poles.
source: However, multiple mutations throughout the protein, including at the C-terminus, have been found to impair localization of endogenous (Farag et al., 2013) or overexpressed (Nicholas et al., 2010, Lim et al., 2015; Sgourdou et al., 2017) mutant WDR62 to the spindle poles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Farag et al., 2013; Nicholas et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2015; Sgourdou et al., 2017).

claim: The WDR62-AURKA interaction requires either the WD-repeat domain at the N-terminus or a middle region (aa 621–1138) of the protein.
source: Mapping studies have suggested the WDR62-AURKA interaction to require either the WD-repeat domain at the N-terminus (Huang et al., 2021) or a middle region (aa 621–1138) (Chen et al., 2014) of the protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Huang et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2014).

claim: The D955AfsX112 mutation is expected to disrupt the middle region (aa 621–1138) of WDR62.
source: The D955AfsX112 mutation is expected to disrupt the latter, as well as the JNK1 phosphorylation site (T1053), previously reported to diminish WDR62 association with the microtubules (Lim et al., 2015); however, the interaction of the mutant protein with AURKA appears preserved, at least in a heterologous overexpression system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the location of the mutation and supported by citation to a published study (Lim et al., 2015).

claim: The D955AfsX112 mutation is expected to disrupt the JNK1 phosphorylation site (T1053), previously reported to diminish WDR62 association with the microtubules.
source: The D955AfsX112 mutation is expected to disrupt the latter, as well as the JNK1 phosphorylation site (T1053), previously reported to diminish WDR62 association with the microtubules (Lim et al., 2015); however, the interaction of the mutant protein with AURKA appears preserved, at least in a heterologous overexpression system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the location of the mutation and supported by citation to a published study (Lim et al., 2015).

claim: Microtubule binding by WDR62 is thought to be mediated by the N-terminal half (aa 1–841).
source: Indeed, although microtubule binding is thought to be mediated by the N-terminal half (aa 1–841) (Lim et al., 2015), our work suggests that the C-terminal half is also needed, even if the mechanism remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Lim et al., 2015).

claim: MCPH-associated C-terminal mutations prevent WDR62 localization to spindle microtubules.
source: This is also in agreement with the observation that MCPH-associated C-terminal mutations prevent WDR62 localization to spindle microtubules (Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Lim et al., 2015).

claim: Disrupted centrosome asymmetry was observed in the Wdr62 gene-trap mouse.
source: Third, we demonstrate that WDR62 regulates mitotic progression and the choice of asymmetric versus symmetric divisions in neural progenitors, reminiscent of disrupted centrosome asymmetry we observed in the Wdr62 gene-trap mouse (Sgourdou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Sgourdou et al., 2017).

claim: Precocious early progenitor delamination and differential effects in early versus late neural progenitor self-renewal and differentiation have been described in Wdr62 gene-trap mice.
source: Of note, precocious early progenitor delamination and differential effects in early versus late neural progenitor self-renewal and differentiation have been described in Wdr62 gene-trap mice (Jayaraman et al., 2016; Sgourdou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Jayaraman et al., 2016; Sgourdou et al., 2017).

claim: At early neurogenic stages, mitotic spindles display more astral microtubules and fewer spindle microtubules, whereas the opposite was observed at later stages.
source: It has been recently reported (Vargas-Hurtado et al., 2019) that at early neurogenic stages, mitotic spindles display more astral microtubules and fewer spindle microtubules, whereas the opposite was observed at later stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Vargas-Hurtado et al., 2019).

claim: During the transition from early to late neurogenesis, WDR62 might be involved in the switch in spindle morphology.
source: As also suggested by others (Huang et al., 2021), it is reasonable to speculate that during the transition from early to late neurogenesis, WDR62 might be involved in the switch in spindle morphology.
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citation to a published study (Huang et al., 2021).

claim: WDR62 dysfunction might impact neurogenic trajectories differentially in the course of neurogenesis, eventually altering the final neuronal output observed in MCPH associated with WDR62 mutations.
source: Thus, WDR62 dysfunction might impact neurogenic trajectories differentially in the course of neurogenesis, eventually altering the final neuronal output observed in MCPH associated with WDR62 mutations, as also suggested by the selective effect in late progenitors we observed in the Wdr62 gene-trap mouse (Sgourdou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citation to a previous study (Sgourdou et al., 2017).
